newsitem.title: JAPAN: S&P says no reason to review ratings for Thailand.
newsitem.headline: S&P says no reason to review ratings for Thailand.

text.p: Despite Thailand's decision to let the baht float, there is no reason to review the country's sovereign ratings, an analyst at Standard & Poor's said on Wednesday.

When asked whether there was any reason to review S&P's ratings for Thailand after the earlier announcements regarding the baht by Thai authorities, Jim Karacadag, sovereign analyst at S&P in New York, said: "The short answer is no."

"At the time we had affirmed the kingdom's sovereign ratings last April, we had clearly stated that the relaxation of the exchange-rate policy would not erode the government's strong financial position to a degree that would impact its creditworthiness," Karacadag told Reuters Financial Television.
"So the answer really is no. We maintain a stable outlook on the foreign currency and local currency rating," he said.

Asked whether the Thai government's plans to provide "soft loans" to businesses would be a concern for sovereign risk, Karacadag said the financial position of the government was strong enough to withstand the burden.
"The Thai government is a strong creditor. It has little debt. Its financial position is very robust and therefore it is in a position to extend that support (to the businesses)," Karacadag said.
Karacadag said uncertainty in the currency market could push Thai interest rates higher in the short term, but benefits could be expected over the long term.
"The Bank of Thailand now has greater monetary policy flexibility because it does not have to live up to the commitment of maintaining the value of the baht," Karacadag said.
"Secondly, once exchange rates stabilise at a new equilibrium, interest rates can be expected to come down, which in turn should relax the burden on the private-sector borrowers," he added.
The impact of a baht depreciation on Thai exports should be positive over the medium term, but it should not be exaggerated, Karacadag said.
"Over time, the volume of exports can be expected to rise. But this should not be exaggerated because a significant proportion of the export sector's inputs are imported."
